FOREWORD 
(to the Third Edition) 
THE Universal Decimal Classification (U.D.C.), originally oerived from the Devvey 
Decimal Classification (D.C.), has been, and is still being, extended for use in classifying 
artic1es in periodicals, monographs and documents of all kinds, under the auspices of the 
Federation Internationale de Documentation (F.I.D.), which authorizes publication of 
various international editions in different languages (see end flyleaf). 
The preparation of the full English edition, parts of which have been already published 
as B.S. 1000, was originally-undertaken by the British Standards Institution at the joint 
request of the British Society for International Bibliography (B.S.I.B.) and the Association 
of Special Libraries and Information Bureaux (A.S.L.I.B.), now amalgamated in Aslib. 
It is the fourth full international edition and has the approval of the Lake Placid Club 
Education Foundation, New York, the body responsible for the Dewey Decimal 
Classification. 
The abridged edition B.S. lOOOA was first published in 1948 ,in response to a widespread 
demand for a comprehensive short edition in English, suitable as an introduction to the 
use of the full schedules and as a manual for classifying books and general documents in 
libraries, for which the full schedules are unnecessarily detailed. It was based on the 
oflicial Dutch abridgment, fifth edition (1946), and owed much to the abridgment published 
in English by H.M. Stationery Office under the title "Classification for Works ill Pure 
and Applied Science in the Science Museum Library," third edition (1936). 
In the radically revised second edition of 1957, account was taken of amendments 
internationally approved and authorized by the F.LD. up to 1955, and the tables corre­
sponded closely to the English text of the Trilingual Abridged Edition B.S. loo0B: 1958, 
the international standard abridged edition of the UD.C. The alphabetical index 
contained over 20,000 entries, as against 2,000 in the first edition, while the terminology 
was revised throughout. Members of the British U.D.C. Committee, together with 
interested specialists too numerous to mention, gave freely of their expert advice and 
criticism, and the ;British Standards Institution takes this opportunity of expressing its 
indebtedness to them and also to the many users all over the world who have made 
suggestions for improving the schedules and the terminology. 
This third edition takes account of the amendments listed in "Extensions and Correc­
tions to the D.D.C." (see p. 254, E) during the four years 1956-59 inclusive, and a few 
further changes in 1960 (up to P-note 700). An outline of new numbers introduced since 
the second edition is given opposite, while cancellations again appear in the text in 
small type 'With marginal asterisks and relocation reference", and, for thor,e made 
since the second edition, the year of cancellation in square brackets.

Note on the Dewey Decimal Classification and the V.D.C. 
The Decimal Classification (D.C.), first published in 1876, 
was designed not only for the arrangement and indexing of 
books on shelves, but also of cards in catalogues, clippings, 
MSS. notes-in fact, of literary material in any form. The 
first edition had only 1,000 headings, but it and later editions 
displayed in their structure many original features, all of 
which were to contribute greatly to the success of the U.D.C. 
The author, Melvil Dewey, described his system as being 
in essence a Subject Classification and a Relative Index. 
He regarded the latter as the most important feature, 
claiming that it solved the great difficulty of classified 
catalogues, i.e. knowit~g just where to put or where to look 
for a particular subject. This was done by displaying clearly, 
in an alphabetical index, the relative aspects of each topic­
aspects which were scattered in the classification according 
to their context, e,.g. sugar in agriculture, in chemical tech­
nology, in cookery, etc. But whirst Dewey showed con­
siderable insight in thus reeognizing that the alphabetical 
relative index is a vital part of a classification, it is the 
structure of his subject classification which is of greatest 
interest to users of the U.D.C. 
The general pattern of the D.C. is as follows: The whole 
field of knowledge is divided into 9 main classes, numbered 
100/900 (U.D.C. classes 1/9), general works constituting a 
tenth class, 000. Each main class is divided into 9 sub­
classes, e.g. class 300 (Social Sciences) into 310/390 (U.D.C. 
31/39). General works on the Social Sciences constitute a 
tenth subclass, divided into 301/309 according to the form 
in which the general subject is presented, e.g. 304 Essays. 
Each subclass is divided into 9 further subclasses, e.g. 320 
(Political Science) into 321/329, general works constituting 
a tenth subclass, divided into 320. 1/320.9. This division 
into ten-may be continued indefinitely-hence "decimal 
classification" . 
U.D.C. users will note that the first 100 classes in the D.C. 
(000, 010 ... 100 ... 990) all have a terminal zero, thus 
maintaining a 3-figure minimum: it has no ordinal 
significance. 
The use of the decimal notation has been one of the most 
successful features of the D.C., offering infinite hospitality 
to new subjects whilst using the best known and simplest of 
symbols-Arabic numerals. It was these two factors, and 
the fact that the D.C. was a classification of subjects, inde­
pendent of language or race, that chiefly determined the 
adoption of the D.C. by the Institut International de 
Bibliographie (I.I.B.) in 1895. Hence, the order of subjects 
in the D.C. and U.D.C. schedules is substantially the same. 
But the D.C. introduced, .in conjunction with its decimal 
notation, two other structural features which have been 
immensely significant in the development of the U.D.C.: 
1. The synthetic principle, whereby recurrent series of 
concepts are arranged in consistent orders and allocated a 
consistent notation. For example, in class 400 (Philology) 
the order of subclasses within each language is the same­
Orthography, Etymology, etc., and the notation representing 
them is also the same, e.g. 425 English grammar, 435 German 
grammar, etc.). The geographical order of countries and 
their divisions is likewise: consistent wherever it is used, 
e.g. 942 British history, 943 German history, 328.42 British 
Legislation, 328.43 German Legislation. 
This synthetic principle clearly results in a mnemonic 
quality; but more important, it greatly increases the scheme's 
possible range of subdivision with no extra cost in printing 
the schedules. So more than 200 different languages can be 
subdivided in detail equal to that provided for the English 
Language, simply by printing the instructions ~'li_de like 
420, English". 
Three fundamental features of the U.D.C. may be directly 
traced to the early synthetic/mnemonic devices of the D.C. 
4 
(i) The Common Auxiliaries are clearly an extension of 
the idea underlying Dewey's Geographic and Form Divi­
sions-i.e. series of divisions recurrent throughout the whole 
field of knowledge. 
(ii) The Special Auxiliaries are clearly an extension of 
Dewey's idea of series recurrent within a particular subject­
e.g. the linguistic divisions under each language. 
(iii) The linking together of main class numbers by means 
of the: (colon) was foreshadowed by certain of the "Divide 
like ... " devices in the D.C., particularly the instruction 
"Divide like the main classification" which appears at 016 
(Subject Bibliographies), at 331.281 (Wages in particular 
industries) in other places. 
2. The usc of a distinctive symbol to introduce a particular 
principle of division. For example, the appearance of a zero 
in a D.C. number usually means that the subject represented 
by the preceding digits is now divided by the principle 
"Form of presentation"; so 677.05 means the subject 
Textile Manufacture 677 presented in the form of a periodical, 
05. Similarly, a zero following a geographic number nearly 
always introduces a period of that place's history. A class 
number so constructed is more flexible than a simple decimal 
number in that it may be expanded at more than one point. 
For example, a Directory of Wool Manufactures is 
677.31058, where both the subject (Textiles 677) and the 
Form Division (Periodicals 05) have been subdivided inde­
pendently of each other. If the form Divisions were not 
introduced by a 0 but were added directly, e.g. .5 instead 
of .05, further division of 677 into types of textile would 
be blocked. 
The great flexibility of the U.D.C. in its use of the 
Auxiliary numbers is a direct result of applying this same 
principle. But where Dewey restricted his notation to 
Arabic numerals, U.D.C. uses other distinctive symbols to 
introduce various auxiliaries. So 677(05) (Periodicals) 
Textiles is similarly expandable to 677.31(058) Wool 
(directories). This use of distinctive symbols enables U.D.C. 
to extend the use of the principle considerably; so where 
D.C. has 822 (English Drama), U.D.C. has 820-2, the 
recurrent concept "Drama" being now introduced by a 
hyphen. As a result, whilst the order of division in the 
Literature class in the D.C. can only be Literature-Language 
-Form-Period-Author (e.g. 822.33 Literature-English 
-Drama-Elizabethan-Shakespear"c), in U.D.C. it could 
be varied, since the numbers for Forms and Periods (and 
Languages too, if necessary) are' distinctively symbolized, 
e.g. 820-2 "1558/1625" (Shakespeare) or 820"155" -<Shake­
speare) or 820 (Shakespeare) or ·even 8-2=20 (Shake-
speare). . _ ' 
It should be clt!arly understood that "decimal classifica­
tion" refers essentially to the structure of the notation, since 
it is theoretically absurd, as Dewey stated; to divide each 
class into just nine subclasses. This means that the 
"expressiveness" of the notation in reflecting co-ordination 
and subordination is often sacrificed. If more than 9 sub­
classes have to be accommodated, some must "share" a 
number, e.g. 941 (Scotland) and 941.5 (Ireland); if less 
than 9 subclasses are required, they are spread over the 
9 numbers, thereby shortening the length of the class 
number-e.g. 592/595 Invertebrates. 
Two distinctive modifications of the D.C. pattern by 
U.D.C. may be noted. Firstly, as an international scheme, 
U.D.C. removes the occasional American emphasis found 
in the D.C. notation-e.g. at 329 (Political Parties). Division 
of any subject by place finds all countries equally provided 
for. Secondly, whilst U.D.C., like D.C., is a general 
classification, not a composite of special classifications, the 
U.D.C. does provide, via its Points-of-view numbers, a 
mechanism whereby the structure of the general scheme may 
be adjusted to the needs of a special classification.

General Introduction 
The Universal Decimal Classification (V.D.C.) is a scheme 
for classifying the whole field of knowledge. It can be 
applied both to the literature which records knowledge, and 
to the catalogues, indexes, etc., which refer to the literature. 
It enables these to be arranged in such a way that all references 
to information on a particular subject can be brought 
together and the information located with the minimum 
of searching. 
Derived some 50 years ago from the Dewey Decimal 
Classification, the system has been steadily amplified and 
modified to cope with the ever-increasing output of recorded 
knowledge in all its branches and forms, but most particularly 
in the fields of science and technology. It has become widely 
accepted internationally as a standard system, and is now 
used in many thousands of libraries and information services 
(for subject cataloguing or indexing, filing and shelving), in 
periodicals (for classifying articles or abstracts), and in 
countless bibliographies and reference lists (for grouping 
individual items by subject). 
The U.D.C. is particularly valuable where exchangeability 
of references is required, as in the joint issue of abstracts or 
informat.ion bulletins by a group of technical organizations, 
01' the distribution of classified index cards through a 
specialized international centre. Because it is so widely 
adopted, previous experience of its use is a real asset, 
especially when new classifiers are appointed or the need 
arises to train new filing staff. Its standard international 
notation, not dependent on anyone alphabet or tongue, 
helps to minimize language difficulties in international 
communication, and may even provide a suitable basis for 
comparative terminology in technical vocabularies, glos­
saries, etc. 
The very universality of the U.D.C. is a challenge to the 
basic conception of all private "specialist" classifications. 
Instead of isolating a particular subject from all other 
specialized fields which, no matter how important, are 
relegated to subsidiary "Miscellaneous ... " or "Other ... " 
headings, there is a serious attempt to recognize each subject 
in its own right, and the specialist is led from his own (often 
narrow) interest to the broader implications in related fields. 
In what follows, an attempt is made to outline the history 
and availability of the U.D.C.; the organization necessary 
for its development and revision; its principles, structure and 
notation; and to provide a few general notes on the use of 
the Main and Auxiliary tables. 
A. HISTORY AND AVAILABILITY 
The idea of using a decimal notation for the subdivisions 
of a library classification originated with Melvil Dewey 
who, after developing and trying out his system for several 
years in the library of Amherst College, Mass. (U.S.A.), 
published the first edition of 24 pages, including index, in 
1876. The value of the classification was soon recognized, 
and its use extended rapidly, first throughout the United 
States and then to the United Kingdom and many parts of 
the British Commonwealth. 
In 1895, following the first International Conference on 
Bibliography, the newly founded Institut International de 
Bibliographie (I.I.B.) sponsored a scheme initiated by two 
Belgian enthusiasts, Paul Otfet and Henri La Fontaine, for 
the establishment of a comprehensive classified index to all 
published information. By arrangement with Melvil Dewey, 
who had just published the 5th edition of his Decimal 
Classification (still no more than a few thousand sub­
divisions), the Ll.B. began expanding the schedules part by 
part, and in 1905 published (in French) the first complete 
5 
international edition of what was later called the Classifica­
tion D6cimale Universelle. Comprising some 33,000 sub­
divisions with an alphabetical index of 38,000 entries, this was 
given the title "Manuel du Repertoire Bibliographique 
Universel" because it provided the basic classification 
schedules for the great card subject-index then being com­
piled in Brussels. 
In following years, the schedules were slowly extended, 
but the First World War interrupted the activity of the 
!.I.B., and it was not until the mid-twenties that work on the 
2nd edition was effectively resumed. The Ll.B. was 
reorganized and its Secretariat established at Deventer in 
Holland, but in 1931 its name was changed to "Institut 
International de Documentation" (U.D.) and its head­
quarters were transferred to The Hague, which is still the 
international U.D.C. centre. By 1937, when the "Institut" 
assumed the present name of "Federation Internationale de 
Documentation" (F.LD.), work had also begun on the 
German and English editions. 
The preparation of the 2nd international edition in­
volved some forty specialists, under the general editorship 
of Otlet and La Fontaine, who were concerned chiefly with 
the HUmanities, and Mr. F. Donker Duyvis (later General 
Secretary of the F.LD.), who was responsible for most of the 
sections on Science and Technology. Containing some 
70,000 subdivisions, this 2nd edition in French was published 
during the years 1927-33 under the title of "Classification 
Decimale Universelle" and has since served as the authori­
tative basis for all subsequent schedules, full and abridged, 
of which a survey is given at the end of this volume. 
Of the three full international editions based on the 
2nd edition, the only one completed since the end of the 
Second World War is the 3rd (German) edition, comprising 
7 volumes of tables and a 3-volume alphabetical index. 
The 4th (English) edition is still in preparation, and the only 
sections so far published are 0, 5, parts of 62 and 67, 669, 
and 69. Rather more has appeared of the 5th edition 
(again in French): namely 0, 2, 3, 61, 62 and 65, but diffi­
culties are being encountered and progress is slow. Other 
editions in Japanese and in Spanish have been begun, and 
one in Portuguese is contemplated. 
Abridged editions have been published in Czech, Dutch, 
English, Finnish, German, Japanese, Polish, Spanish, 
Swedish and other languages, while Arabic and Portuguese 
editions are in preparation. Only a very brief outline 
schedule exists. in French, but a standard abridged text is 
included in the important new 3-Ianguage edition issued 
jointly by the Deutscher Normenausschuss (D.N.A.) and the 
British Standards Institution (B.S.!.), with the Association 
Beige de Documentation (A.B.D.) and the Union Fran<;aise 
des Organismes de Documentation (U.F.O.D.). 
Special "selection" or "excerpt" schedules have recently 
appeared: notably, one for Architects, Builders and Civil 
engineers (A.B.C.), and a German "Fachausgabe" for 
"Measurement, testing, control and protection". Similar 
editions for other specialized fields are in preparation or 
contemplated. 
B. DEVELOPMENT AND REVISION 
The development and maintenance of a system as compre­
hensive and widely used as'the U.D.C. could hardly have 
been achieved without some form of effective supervision 
and control. The ultimate authority on general U.D.C. 
policy and development is the International Committee on 
Universal Classification, on which all national member com­
mittees of the F.LD. are entitled to be represented, but its 

--- PAGE 6 ---
membership is too diffuse to maintain continuity between 
F.I.D. Conferences. Day-to-day control and supervision are 
vested in the more compact Central Classification Com­
mittee (C.C.C.), which consists of the F.I.D. General 
Secretary and the editors of the full V.D.C. editions (Ger­
man, English, French, Japanese, Spanish) ex .officio. 
These editors are in close and constant touch with the 
F.I.D. General Secretariat at The Hague, where an up-to­
the-mimlte master copy of the complete U.D.C. is main­
tained, based on proposals submitted by V.D.C. revision 
committees or individuals in many parts of the world. 
In revi<;ion, conflicting tendencies are inevitable: the older 
established users, having built up extensive U.D.C. cata­
logues over tha years, tend to resist changes, whilst the 
newer and prospective ones, with little or no existing U.D.C.­
classified material, are often anxious for drastic rearrange­
ment, sometimes in the interests of logic alone. However, 
the majority of those active in U.D.C. revision have accepted 
a policy of compromise: they endeavour to make the 
classification better for established users, and more attractive 
to non-users; to reduce confusions and shortcomings, and 
to introduce new concepts without disturbing the existing 
tables too much. 
The governing rule in all U.D.C. revision work is that the 
significance of a particular number may be extended or 
restricted, but may not be completely altered. If a U.D.C. 
number (with any subdivisions) is obsolete, it may be 
"canceJlcd", which means that its use is no longer authorized 
because a better or more up-to-date arrangement has been 
developed under another number, often a "free" (unused) 
number. Eventually, the cancelled number becomes "free" 
(by disuse) and may then be authorized with a completely 
different significance, but only after a period of 10 years, 
which is considered the minimum nccessary to enable current 
users to readjust their files and to avoid widespread confusion 
of the older and newer meanings. This policy undoubtedly 
slows down revision, but probably creates least dissatis­
faction, especially when applied with discretion and some 
degree of flexibility. 
C. PRINCIPLES 
Three basic principles are evident in the Univc.rsal Decimal 
Classification :-
I. It is a classification in the strictest sense, depending 
on the analysis of idea content, so that related concepts 
and groups of cOllcepts are brought together, and the 
arbitrary and often haphazard systematization of alpha­
betical and other arrangements is avoided. 
2. It is a universal classification in that an attempt is made 
to include in it every field of knowledge, not as a patchwork 
of isolated, self-sufficient specialist groupings, but as an 
integrated pattern of correlated subjects. This universality 
at the conceptual level is supported by notational devices, 
which permit the linking of simple main numbers (for simpJe 
ideas) either with other main numbers or with auxiliaries 
denoting Place, Time and similar commonly recurring 
categories-in each case forming combined or compound 
numbers. If separate index entries are made under each 
single main number forming part of a combined number, 
the complex subject can be located from each point of view, 
regardless of any subjective approach on the part of the 
classifier. 
3. It is a universal decimal claSSification, constructed on 
the principle of proceeding from the general to the more 
particular by the (arbitrary) division of the whole of human 
knowledge into ten main branches, each further subdivided 
decimally to the required degree. This principle can be 
applied to any notation, but Arabic numerals are inter-
6 
nationally familial' in a recognized order, whercas letters and 
other symbols arc not. 
The U.D.C. is essentially a practical system for numerically 
coding information, so designed that any item, once coded 
and filed correctly, can be readily found from whatever 
angle it is sought. It should not be regarded as a philo­
sophical classification of knowledge, nor is the order of 
subjects of primary importance. What is of greater moment 
to a scientific classification is that the introduction of an 
auxiliary apparatus of connection and relation signs, lacking 
in the original Dewey system, has made the U.D.C. really 
universal, in the sense that it permits almost any desired 
combination and modification of basic numbers to denote 
the most complex SUbjects. (Se~ D 2 !tIld F.) 
D.l. STRUCTURE. NOTATION 
The whole field of human knowledge, regarded as 
unity, is divided into tcn main branches denoted by decimal 
fractions as follows:-
.0 Generalities: methodology, documentation, scripts; 
recording, collection and dissemination of information 
. I Philosophy, metaphysics, logic, ethics. Psychology 
.2 Religion. Theology 
.3 Social sciences: including statistics, law, education 
.4 Philology. Languages 
.5 Pure science, mathematical and natural 
.6 Applied science: medicine and technology 
.7 The Arts, including architecture, photography, 
entertainment and sport 
.8 Literature 
.9 Geography. Biography. History 
On this foundation, the notation is built up by continuous 
extension of the decimal fractions, on the principle of 
proceeding from the general to the particular. Thus, every 
concept within the domain of pure science is represented by 
a decimal fraction greater than .5 and less than .6, the sub­
divisioil being carried to any required degree, as shown by 
the following example: 
.5 Pure science, mathematical and natural 
.51 Mathematics 
.52 Astronomy, geodesy 
.53 Physics, with mechanics 
.531 Mechanics (of solid bodies) 
.531 7 Measurement of geometrical and mechanical 
.53 I 71 
.532 
magnitudes 
Measurement of length, linear dimensions 
Fluid mechanics 
etc. etc. 
For convenience, the initial decimal point is omitted, though 
it is the fact that all U.D.C. numbers are in reality decimal 
fractions less than unity that determines the sequence of 
numbers, which otherwise would seem chaotic. On the 
other hand, purely as a visual aid, "points" are inserted 
usually after every third figure. Thus, in the example above, 
the numbers. 53 onwards are written 53,531,531.7,531.71, 
etc., and so they are given throughout the main tables. 
Only when introducing the .00 and .0 auxiliaries [see 
Tables (i) and (k)], or for some specific mnemonic purpose, 
such as the parallel division of91 and the (4) to (9) auxiliaries, 
e.g. 91.44 Geography of France, is the position of the point 
varied. Generally, however, any such deviation from the 
usual triple-figure pattern does not affect the filing order of 
the numbers. 
Logical classification seldom requires regular step-by-step 
subdivision into ten. Usually, there are fewer than ten sub­
divisions, and a number of places are left "free" for possible 
future use. On the rare occasions when more than ten are 

--- PAGE 7 ---
needed, centesimal (instead of decimal) division is resorted 
to, e.g. under 354 Ministries; or, to shorten notation, a single 
subject may be spread over several divisions, e.g. 596/599 
Vertebrates. 
From the foregoing brief outline of the notational structure 
of the main U.D.C. tables, it will be clear that every subject, 
however long its number, is included (by implication) in a 
parent number, so that the degree of precision in classifying 
may be adjusted to the needs of the individual user. Thus, 
to continue the example already mentioned, a user with a 
collection of books mainly on literature and the arts (U.D.C. 
7 and 8) might find the nu'mber 53 (or even 5) adequate, 
whereas one with more special interest in Physics and the 
natural sciences might have to assign the full number 
531.7, for a book on "Mechanical Measuring Devices", or 
at least 531, to differentiate his group of books on Mechanics 
from others on Optics or other branches of Physics. 
The continuous step-by-step extension by decimal sub­
division is clearly shown in the full-page Example (p. 8) 
in which one particular branch of Applied Science, 6, is 
followed through 62, 621, 621.3 to the 5th figure. 
D.2. AUXILIARY NOTATION 
In practice, the subject-matter or content of a document 
is not always so simple and clear-cut, and may require more 
than a simple decimal number for easy retrieval by users 
with different approaches. The subject-matter may be: 
(a) A complex fusion of two or more independently 
classifiable concepts, denoted by linking the appropriate 
main numbers by the: (colon) sign for relationship, e.g. 
Heat treatment of steel 621.785: 669.14 
Physical basis of music 534 : 781 
(b) A detailed element, attribute or aspect of any main 
subject denotable by a simple main decimal number and not 
normally classifiable without reference to that number, e.g. 
Architectural styles 72.03 
Steel strips 669.14-418 
Rubber research 678.001.5 
Shipbuilding in England 629.12(42) 
In classification schemes designed for specialists in par­
ticular fields, such common concepts as "styles", "strips" 
and "research" may be given arbitrary subdivisions under 
the appropriate heads, but in a comprehensive general 
system designed to cover the whole of knowledge, or a large 
part of it, this would mean endless repetition and sheer waste 
of paper and print. 
In the U.D.C., the problem is solved by the provision of 
an Auxiliary notation of special signs and numbers, listed in 
one set of tables (a) to (k) but applicable as needed to all 
parts Of the main tables. These serve to distinguish, not only 
the finer details and complexities of the subject-matter or 
content of a document, but also the language or other form 
in which it is presented. They should only be used when the 
main tables are inadequate. 
The use of Auxiliaries (and compound numbers) is briefly 
outlined in the last section of this Introduction (F), and 
further explanations and directives are given with the 
abridged lists in the Auxiliary tables which immediately 
follow it.

NOTES ON USING THE u'D.C. 
Classification is something of an art, and proficiency in it 
depends as much on a general background knowledge of the 
SUbject-matter to be classified as on a broad grasp of the 
principles and notation of the system in use. For a scheme 
as comprehensive and flexible as the UD.C., it is almost 
impossible to lay down any rigid rules, and all that is here 
attempted is to offer a few general hints on how to set about 
classifying in such a way as to render the contents of books, 
periodicals and other documents most accessible to those in 
search of information. 
1. Start by assessing the needs of the potential users: what 
range of information will be looked for, and from what points 
of view, and what additional sources are likely to be 
acquired as time goes on. Always keep these points in mind 
when assigning U.D.C. numbers to individual documents. 
2. Faced with large numbers of documents, try to sort them 
into manageable piles according to very broad subject groups, 
perhaps reserving a special pile for the more "difficult" ones 
whic.h do not obviously fall into any of these groups and 
therefore need more careful consideration. 
3. For papers already classified, check U.D.C. numbering 
to ensure that it is compatible with personal practice. The 
original classifier may have been content with much broader 
numbering than is now required, or may have had in mind 
a ditTerent group of readers or users. 
4. In detennining the subject, never rely on the title alone. 
Glance inside every document, look through the synopsis or 
contents list and, if necessary, rapidly scan the text. Even 
the most lucid and apparently explanatory title may not 
convey some aspect or feature vital for the particular users 
in question. 
5. To detcnnine the D.D.C. number(s), never rely on the 
printed index alone: always verify in the systematic tables. 
The alphabetical index is an invaluable preliminary aid, but 
for correct and accurate placing, due regard must be paid to 
the broad headings and cognate subdivisions in the tablcs 
themselves. 
6. Avoid classifying too minutely, unless expecting a rapid 
growth in the collection. Over-detailed subdivision is 
unecollomical: it means longer numbers, and may needlessly 
segregate items in an already compact group, when they 
might be better arranged by dates of publication or by names, 
of authors or by a combination of both. 
7. Do not hesitate to assign two or Dlore D.D.C. numbers 
if the document presents several distinct subjects or aspects 
of a subject, and usc the : (colon) freely to link related 
concepts. Avoid the other connecting signs + and / 
wherever possible: filing and retrieval are simpler and 
quicker if separate entries are made for each U.D.C. number 
assigned. 
8. If two or more U.D.C. numbers seem equally applicable 
to a subject, choose the one which corresponds most closely 
to the users' requirements. Where no clear choice is possible, 
assign the number first in U.D.C. numerical sequence, or 
enter also under the alternative number(s). 
9. For permancnt collections, build up a detailed alpha­
betical subject-index in conjunction with the main classified 
catalogue. Maintain it regularly, checking for accul'acy and 
completeness as each item is assigned its U.D.C. number, 
and use it to display subsidiary aspects of all main h~adings 
(as suggested in Fl). At the same time make duplicate cards 
or slips, arranging them in classified order to show what 
subject headings have already been allocated to the U.D.C. 
numbers used. 
10. To maintain a well-adjusted, up-to-date classified file, 
check it periodically against the authorized "Extensions and 
Corrections to the V.D.C."-if possible, every 6 months as 
issued, but at least every three years when the last issue 
(No.6) of each series appears.

F. USE OF AUXILIARIES AND CO:MPOUND 
NUMBERS 
Auxiliaries are a means of eliminating repetition in all 
parts of the printed main tables, in that they group certain 
recurring and generally subordinate concepts, such as 
Language, Form, Place, Time and Point of View-cf. Tables 
(c) to (i). They do not stand alone, but are attached to main 
u.n.c. numbers denoting primary subject-matter. 
An auxiliary should not be used for a concept which can 
be denoted by a simple main number, or by two such 
numbers linked by colon: (sign of relation). For example, 
a document on "African Rivers" should not be classified 
916(282) or 551.482(6), when 916: 551. 482 will ensure that 
it is indexed under both Gcography of Africa and Hydro­
graphy of rivers. One on "River life (plants, animals)", 
however, is adequately classified 577.47(282), since the 
information is clearly ecological and not hydrographic. 
In practice it will be found that it is seldom necessary to 
use more than one auxiliary, unless very minute subdivision 
is required: usually, colon linkage and the ( ... ) series will 
suffice. Choice and order are dealt with at the end of this 
section F. 
t. Special auxiliary subdivisions and "hiding" information 
In many sections of the main tables, it is found con· 
venient to provide more specialized subdivisions: each series 
specific to a particular subject or its related fields where 
indicated. These can serve as fixed main numbers when 
used as they stand (attached to the base-number), or they 
may be detached and added to any of its direct decimal 
divisions, if regarded as subordinate, e.g. 
677 Textiles industry 
.052 Spinning machines (in general) 
677.21 Cotton industry 
.052 Cotton-spinning machines 
A concept which seems subordinate to one group of 
specialists, however, may be of primary importance to 
another. It follows that the use of .0 and - ... subdivisions, 
detached from the fixed base-number and scattered under its 
various subdivisions, may easily lead to the "hiding" of 
concepts which ought to be independently retrievable. 
Thus, to follow up the example mentioned, if documents 
dealing with special spinning machines for flax, cotton, etc., 
are indexed only under the respective industries (677.11.052, 
677.21 .052, etc.), and not under 677.052 also, then informa­
tion on Spinning machines which may be of interest to the 
machinery makers will be "hidden", because the special 
kinds of spinning machines have been treated as subordinate 
to the flax, cotton or other industries. 
This applies especially to abstracts or other lists, in which 
the items are only broadly classified and the alphabetical 
subject index (if any) contains only the general headings. 
In library catalogues, the subordinate aspects of each 
heading may be effectively and economically displayed in the 
detailed alphabetical-subject"index built up by the classifier 
for the particular collection: in the example quoted, there 
will be no real need for second entries under 677.052, since 
the scattered information will be brought together in the 
alphabetical index as follows: 
Spinning machines 
cotton 
flax 
wool 
677.052 
677.21.052 
677.11.052 
677.3.052 
2. Reversal of component parts of compound U.D.C. numbers 
It may be desirable, in a file or list, to bt. able to find 
quickly all available information relating to, say, a particular 
A* 9 
country or region, or some special date or period, or even 
all documents issued in a certain form or a certain language. 
Where pUllched cards or other mechanical selection systems 
are not in use, such information can readily be brought 
together by reversing the normal order of main number and 
auxiliary and making duplicate entry under the auxiliary. 
Thus, Mining in Belgium 622(493) may also be written 
(493)622 for insertion in a duplicate file of (1/9) numbers 
in which each country or regional division will be subdivided 
by the main U.D.C. numbers corresponding to the whole 
range of its social, industrial, cultural and other activities. 
To avoid having to type the full entries separately for the 
two or more cards required (simply to secure the CDrrect 
u.n.c. number order on each), the cards may be prepared 
in one operation, all exactly alike, and the appropriate part 
of the compound number underlined on each card, e.g. 
622(493) for filing under 622, and 
622(~) for filing under (493). 
The same practice may also be followed with colon-I~ked 
numbers, and even with Special - ... and .0 subdivisions 
detached from the normal base-number and used with direct 
decimal divisions of it, as explained in Table (k), part B. 
3. Intercalation 
.Certain Common auxiliaries (Place, Time) are provided 
With double (open and close) signs, which lend themselves 
readily to intercalation, e.g.

(42) England

"18" 19th century

music 
Intercalation, though permitting utmost flexibility and any 
desired grouping, has an individualistic quality making it more 
suitable for private use, and should be avoided altogether 
when classifying data for wider circulation or exchange. 
4. Choice of suitable auxiliaries: priority. preference 
As mentioned, more than one auxiliary is seldom neces­
sary, especially when applied in cOdjunctlon with the 
: (colon) sign. Selection of the most suitable auxiliary 
depends on the requirements of the specialist user and the 
choice will generally fall on the series which most restricts 
the scope of the subject-matter denoted by the main number. 
Only where further minute definition is essential should 
additional auxiliaries be used. 
In sections of tl1e main tables provided with Special -... 
or .0 or ' ... s'lbdivisions, one of these will usually be the 
obvious choice. Where there are none, or where those 
mentioned are unsuitable, use may be made of One of the 
series of Common auxiliaries, of which the most generally 
helpful are the .00 Point-of-view series, and the (1/9) Place 
and" ... " Time auxiliaries. Apart from these which relate 
to subject content, there are two series di5ti~guishing the 
Form (0 .•. ) and Language = ... in which a document 
may be presented. 
5. Intcrnal order of auxiliaries in a compound number 
When two or more auxiliaries have to be used with a simple 
main number. their internal or "horizontal" order in the 
resulting compound number is decided by the order in which 
they have been selected: that is, the most significant (usually 
the most restrictive) first. Although "significance" may vary

(a) Addition and consecutive extension signs + and I 
The + ("plus" or "and") sign may be used to connect 
two or more separated (non-consecutive) V.D.C. numbers, 
especially when these denote commonly associated concepts 
or the same broad subject in different aspects, for which no 
single comprehensive number exists. 
e.g. 622 + 669 Mining and metallurgy 
59 + 636 Zoology and animal breeding 
(46) + (72) + (8) Spain, Mexico and South America 
(Spain and Latin America) 
A reference thus classified is filed under each of its con­
stituent numbers, which may indeed be written separately, 
if preferred, one below the other (i.e. without the + sign at 
ali), especially when they denote distinct concepts, not 
commonly associated, but arbitrarily included in a single 
paper or document. 
For simplicity and economy, general or comprehensive 
studies of a subject figuring under several sections of the 
classification may be designated by the D.D.C. number which 
comes first in decimal sequence, followed by the + sign alone, 
e.g. 159.9 + Psychology (individual, social, industrial, 
medical) 
582.28+ Fungi (biology and distribution; cultivation; 
uses, medicinal and industrial) 
However, omission of the further numbers after the + sign 
may mean that, for instance, medical workers accustomed to 
finding all relevant information on medical psychology 
under 616.89 will fail to find some valuable information in a 
paper classified under 159.9 +, and it is safer, therefore, to 
add all the numbers or at least provide permanent cross­
references to these. 
Tile I (strol{e) sign, meaning "from ... to ... " is used to 
join the first and last of a series of consecutive V.D.C. numbers 
denoting a range of concepts which collectively form a broad 
subject or branch of knowledge, for which no single compre­
hensive number exists, 
e.g. 59U599 Systematic zoology (equivalent to 
592+593+ ... 599) 
624/628 Civil engineering (equivalent to 
624+625-1-... 628) 
(b) Relation sign: 
The: (colon) sign, most important·of the'~e~ting sym­
bols, is used generally to link two or more U.D.C."numbers 
denoting related concepts of (approximately) equal value, 
the numbers being reversed to ensure separate entries for 
the co-ordinate ideas. 
10 
e.g. 17:7 
31:63

Statistics applied to agriculture, agri­
cultural statistics (reversed as 63: 31) 
341.63(44:45) Arbitration between Franco (44) and 
Italy (45)

Typing duplicate cards for files, purely for the sake of the 
reversed numbers, may be avoided by using carbon replicas 
and underlining the appropriate component, 
e.g. 17: 7 for filing under 7 
341 :63(44:45) for filing under (44:45) 
341.63(44:45) for filing under (45:44) 
Practical considerations call for maximum use of this sign, 
and wherever doubt arises, it should be preferred to the 
+ (plus) sign. Its significance, indeed, is not limited to a 
strictly co-ordinate relationship, and it may be used to 
separate several U.D.C. numbers which, for clarity and to 
avoid long combinations, may be written one below the 
other, 
e.g. 669.1: 543 Iron and steel: analysis 
: 546.22 Sulphur (in iron and steel) 
:546.815 Lead (in iron and steel) 
When the relationship involves a subordinate· concept for 
which no separate entry is required by reversal, square 
brackets [ ], or « » on typewriters, may be used in place 
of the colon 
e.g. 620.174[669.14] Materials testing-bend tests (for steel) 
This symbol lends itself to intercalation, thus permitting 
alternative grouping, 
e.g. 620.1 [669.14]74 Materials testing (for steel)-bend tests 
but it is a refinement which may usually be dispensed with, 
especially in printed or other widely circulated publications, 
for which the: (colon) should be preferred.

(e) Common auxiliaries of Place (1/9) 
These serve to indicate the geographical range of the 
subject denoted by the preceding main number, 
e.g. 347.77(492) Dutch patent law 
385(43) The German railway system 
When the geogr&phical or regional aspect is paramount, 
entry may be made under the auxiliary, which then precedes 
the main number, 
e.g. (492)347.77 Netherlands, patent law 
(43)385 Germany, its railway system 
12 
The closed symbol ( ... ) lends itself to intercalation, and it is 
often helpful to interpose the auxiliary after the first two 
figures, or in another preferred position, provided the entry 
under the main (subject) number is retained. 
Relation between, and association of, places may be 
expressed by means of the connection signs (Tables a and b) 
inside the brackets, the specifying numbers being reversible, 
e.g. (43: 44) Germany and (in relation to) France 
(7/8) The Americas (considered together) 
(41 + 73) Britain and (together with) America (U.s.A.)

(g) Common Auxilh.ries of Time ".oo" 
These serve to specify date, period 01' other time aspects 
of the subject denoted by the preceding (main) number, 
except 571 Prellistory, ill which a special series (I I ... ) is 
used. For dates, the ordinary calendar reckoning notation is 
placed between inverted commas in the order-Year, Month, 
Day, e.g. 
"1898. 12. 11" (11th December 1898) 
"1930.06.05" (5th June 1930) 
This "four-twa-two" pattern makes for greater clarity in 
extensive arrays of cards or listed items, and reduces the 
risk of confusion with the "3" to "7" timc concepts and of 
reverse interpretation of year and day, which might easily 
occur with the first two figures oll1itted. Thus, if the second 
example above were written "30.06. 05", the date might 
be rcad as 30th June 1905. It is to maintain the "four­
two-two" pattern that the nought(s) must be inserted, even 
for dates between the years 0 and 999, c.g. 
"0435. OB. 04" (4th August, 1\.0. 435) 
Dates before the birth of Christ (!J.e.) are distinguished by 
prefixing the - (minus sign), e.g. 
"-0064" (In the year 64 Il.C.) 
The + (plus) is prefixed only when contrasting A.D. dates 
or periods, ill a series beginning Il.C., e.g. 
"+0090" (In the year A.D. 90) 
Centuries or decades arc denoted by 2- or 3·figurc notations 
respectively, e.g. 
"03" 
"19" 
"191" 
"193" 
4th century (the 300s) 
20th centu ry (the 1900s) 
Second decade (1910-19) 
The "thirties" (1930-39) 
Periods embracing scveral centuries, decades or years are 
denoted by the initial and final figures, separated by the 
/ sign, e.g. 
"16/18" 17th to 19th cen turics 
"187/189" The "seventies", "eighties" and "nineties" 
"1919/1939" The "inter-war" years (1919 to 1939) 
The Common Auxiliaries of Time arc used to designate 
date, period 01' other time aspects of the subject-l1lutter Or 
content denoted by the main U.D.C. number, and not date 
of pUblication or issue.

(h) Alphabetical and (non-decimal) Numerical Subdivision 
The main U.D.C. tables, with the various Auxiliaries, 
serve to group subjects, but not to specify individual I\umes 
or numbers. To do this, the appropriate names or initials 
(in brackets, if desired) and/or numerals have to be added. 
the latter being distinguished, where necessary, from the 
U.D.C. decimal numbering by a prefixed "No." 
E.g. 061.5 Firms, businesses, etc.

(i) Common Auxiliaries of Point of view .00 ..• 
These .00 numbers, added to any main U.D.C. number, 
indicate the broader aspects of a particular subject, each of 
the subdivisions. 001/.009 providing a distinct, but compre­
hensive, approach to the whole field, e.g. 
622 Mining: industry, engineering, etc. 
.001 Programme, research, development 
.002 Production and technique problems 
.003 Commercial and financial aspects 
.005 Equipping and installation problems 
.006 Pit location, accommodation, etc. 
.007 Manpower and personnel problems 
.008 Administration and management (of the mine) 
They are never used alone, but always added to a main 
number, and should not be confused with the main u'D.C. 
divisions 001/009 (Generalities: methodology, documenta­
tion, etc.). 
Any of the Common auxiliaries of Time, Place, Form and 
Language may be added if required, but the wider implica­
tions of each aspect are denoted by extensive coloning to 
other U.D.C. main numbers, e.g. 
622.007:331.69 Shortage of labour in the mines 
: 331.88 Mineworkers' union organization 
When there are relatively few items to be classified, 
direct coloning (without the .00.. numbers) may suffice: 
the order of the coloned numbers may not be entirely satis­
factory, but the shorter notation will compensate for this. 
When documents or references to the literature arc numerous, 
however, and especially if they have to be classified from a 
more subjective viewpoint than ihat permitted by the 
relatively objective systematization of the UD.C. main 
tables, direct coloning may create an unsatisfactory, and \" 
even chaotic, order of the subdivisions, which can be avoided ' 
by judicious use of ,00 numbers. 
For instance, in a water engineering institution [628. I], 
having a large collection of documents of purely internal 
interest, direct coloning to main numbers would yield a some­
what haphazard arrangement, as shown in the following 
examples: 
628 . 1 : 022. 5 
:069 
: 331. 8 
:368.4 
:543.3 
:659.24 
:663.63 
Public reading room 
Museum 
Working hours, conditions of personnel 
Workmen's insurance 
Water analysis 
Information bureau 
Water purification 
This arrangement, in the natural order of the coloned main 
numbers, is clearly unsatisfactory, and a much better "array" 
23 
could be obtained by suitable grouping with the aid of a 
few .00 numbers, thus: 
628.1.002: Waterworks practice, water supply, etc. 
: 543.3 Analysis of water supply 
: 663.63 Purification of water supply 
.005 Equipment and installation problems 
: 022. 5 Pu blic reading room 
:069 Museum 
: 659.24 Information bureau 
.007 Personnel, staff problems 
:331.8 Working hours, conditions 
: 368.4 Insurance matters 
In private use, the formidable notation so created can be 
simplified by substituting a letter or some other conventional 
symbol for the full U.D.C. number for the organization (or 
its main subject), thus: 
X.002:543.3 
X.007:331.8 
but this practice should not be adopted in published lists, 
catalogues, etc., unless the significance of the symbol is 
clearly stated, e.g. in a footnote.

(k) Special (auxiliary) Subdivisions -.. 0, .0 ... and ".0 
A. Role and range of application. Whereas the Common 
auxiliaries represent subordinate ideas recurring in every 
field of knowledge, and each table or series, having its own 
distinctive sign, is applicable to all sections of the main 
tables, these - (hyphen), .0 and ' (apostrophe) subdivisions 
are more specialized in their scope, and each series is limited 
to use in the section for which it is designed or in related 
sections as indicated. This limitation is also necessary 
because two of the signs, (hyphen) and .0 (point 0), have to 
do duty for numerous distinct categories of ideas in different 
sections of the main tables. For instance, -3 is used in 
quite ditTerent senses under 54. 621 and 622, whilst .05 is 
used with an even greater variety of meanings under 06, 22, 
331, 34, 53, 624, 654, 656 and the main divisions of 66, 
67 and 7. 
Of the two kinds of "analytical" subdivisions, the - .. 
are generally more widely applicable than any .0 series in 
the domains of science and technology. The important 
se(ies -1/-9 listed under. 621, for instance, with certain 
exceptions noted, is extensively applied in all sections· of 6 
(other than 61), e.g.

Less widely applicable, however, arc the various series of

B. Use as "main" nllmbers for improved retrieval of 
information. In so far as they represent subordinate aspects 
of a main subject, the Special - .. and .0 subdivisions are 
used in the same way as the Common auxiliaries, i.e. detached 
from the main base-number under which they are listed, and 
affixed to any of its decimal subdivisions .. 1 to .. 9, as 
shown in the examples already given. However, they may 
denote important features of the main subject for which 
25 
there may be no other suitable mam decimal division 
.. 1/ .. 9, and simply to detach and scatter them under a 
variety of subordinate headings would be to "hide" informa­
tion, which should be retrievable under one general number 
(cl. FI). In such circumstances, unless a detailed alpha­
betical index has been built up to provide for adequate 
retrieval (c/ E9 and Fl), the Special suhdivisions should 
be used as they stand, i.e. attached to the main number they 
are listed under, a second entry being made when the concept 
denoted by the -.. or .0 .. refers to a specific decimal 
division of that main base-number. This may be done by 
using the : (colon) sign (c/ Table b) to form a compound 
number, the two components of which may be reversed in 
the usual way, e.g. 
621-52 :621.74 Automatic control in foundries 
[621.74:621-52] 
677 . 052: 677 . 2 I Cotton-spinning machines 
[677 . 21 : 677 .052] 
Alternatively, and more accurately, the double entry may be 
effected by writing the two numbers (in full) one below the 
other, or writing only the one compound number (as for 
Common auxiliaries), and using some simple convention, 
such as underlining, to mark the parts to be juxtaposed for 
the second entry, e.g. 
{
677.052 Spinning machines 
677 .21.052 Cotton-spinning machines 
01' 677.21. 052 (meaning "file also under 677.052") 
C. The apostrophe' .•. , most recent addition to U.D.C. 
auxiliary notation, is synthetic-not analytical-in function; 
in a way which is logical and clearly seen to be so, it serves 
to build up the compound number for a substance (or other 
entity) derived from two or more components by inte­
grating the relevant "component" subdivisions with an 
"umbrella" base-number meaning "composition" (e.g. 
666.113) or by accreting some secondary "component" 
subdivision(s) to a base-number denoting the primary com­
ponent (e.g. 546.32). 
Although it may introduce a series independently designed 
for a particular base-number (e.g. the ' 1/ '7 subdivisions of 
678.6-not detailed in this edition), the apostrophe usually 
replaces certain main-number figures common to each 
component, e.g. the 546 in both the '41 and '28 of 
666 . I 13 '41 '28 Lime-silica glass, or the 669 itself in the '5 
and '6 of 669.35 '5'6 Cu-Zn-Sn alloys. 
When an '... series is added to a base-number which 
has no direct decimal division, the resulting compound 
numbers are filed as straightforward main-number divisions 
(see D.1., p. 6); when added to a base number which has 
further direct divisions, however, the '... series is filed 
immediately before them (see F.6, p. 10), e.g. 
547.29 '26 Carboxy-acid esters 
'262 Ethyl esters 
.292 '26 Acetates (in general) 
'262 Ethyl acetate

*E. EXTENSIONS 
The "Extensions and Corrections to the U.D.C." are 
issued half-yearly and cumulated in' 3-year series (of (; 
numbers each). No sectional lists are available, but the 
contents arranged in broad U.D.C. groups keep thl 
published editions up to date. The subscription is 4 guineas 
annually.
